# The provenance file on Belobog

*The provenance file for Belobog. Nothing here is unsourced; that is what the file is for.*

## Provenance

**1. The attestation.** **—**, from the tradition's own record. On record: Cosmas of Prague, Chronica Boemorum I.4 (c. 1125), Helmold of Bosau, Chronica Slavorum I.52 (c. 1172), Gieysztor, Mitologia Słowian (1982), Rosik, Białobóg na ziemiach słowiańskich (2013).

**2. The narrative record.** **Zeloboch of the Czech Chronicle** — The only medieval author to name Belobog is Cosmas of Prague, whose Chronica Boemorum (c.  1125, Book I. **Chernobog at Rethra** — Belobog's structure is completed by his opposite.  Helmold of Bosau (Chronica Slavorum I.

**3. The physical record.** There is no archaeology of Belobog: no image, temple, or inscription bearing his name has been found, and no Slavic sanctuary excavated to date can be assigned to him. The great Slavic cult sites belong to other gods — Arkona's temple of Svetovid on Rügen (destroyed 1168, described by Saxo Grammaticus), the debated 'Rethra' of Helmold's Black God — and the famous carved idols (the Zbruch pillar) name no deity at all. Belobog's evidence is documentary (Cosmas, Helmold) and ethnographic (the harvest-wreath records). The absence is not trivial: it means the White God belongs to that large class of ancient deities known only through the words of their adversaries — a god whose temples were wooden, seasonal, and gone.

**4. The current holding.** The temple at [/belobog/](/belobog/), classified Tier 2. One decisive feature survives — a single, honest mark — which places the restoration in Tier-2: exact, and exactly labeled.

**5. The documented resonances.** **Finance, Wealth & Commerce**, **Retail & Marketplaces**, **Startups & Venture Creation** — seats argued and weighted in the [pattern atlas](/patterns/), read through the myths in this temple's [Resonance File](/belobog/blog/resonance/).

**6. The continuing record.** Belobog's name lives wherever Slavic says 'white': in Bělehrad — Belgrade, 'the White City' — and in a family of names and words built on the same root.  His cultural afterlife, though, belongs to the modern era.
